In Exercises 19–28, all vectors are in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ . Mark each statement True or False (T/F). Justify each answer.

problem.paragraph: (T/F) If the distance from $$\mathbf{u}$$ to $$\mathbf{v}$$ equals the distance from $$\mathbf{u}$$ to $$- \mathbf{v}$$ , then $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ are orthogonal.

(T/F) If vectors $$\mathbf{v}_{1}$$ , $$\ldots$$ , $$\mathbf{v}_{p}$$ , span a subspace $$W$$ and if $$\textbf{x}$$ is orthogonal to each $$\mathbf{v}_{j}$$ for $$j = 1,\ldots,p,$$ then $$\textbf{x}$$ is in $$W^{\bot}$$ .
(T/F) If $$\textbf{x}$$ is orthogonal to every vector in a subspace $$W$$ then $$\textbf{x}$$ is in $$W^{\bot}$$ .
(T/F) For a square matrix $$A$$ , vectors in $$\text{Col} A$$ are orthogonal to vectors in $$\text{Nul} A$$ .
(T/F) For an $$m \times n$$ matrix $$A$$ , vectors in the null space of $$A$$ are orthogonal to vectors in the row space of $$A$$ .
Use the transpose definition of the inner product to verify parts (b) and (c) of Theorem 1. Mention the appropriate facts from Chapter 2.
Let $$\mathbf{u} = \left( u_{1} \text{,} u_{2} \text{,} u_{3} \right)$$ . Explain why $$\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{u} \geq 0$$ . When is $$\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{u} = 0$$ ?

Let $$\mathbf{u} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 2 \\ {- 5} \\ {- 1} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ and $$\mathbf{v} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 7} \\ {- 4} \\ 6 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . Compute and compare $$\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}$$ , $$\text{∥} \textbf{u} \text{∥} ^{2}$$ , $$\text{∥} \textbf{v} \text{∥} ^{2}$$ , and $$\text{∥} \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} \text{∥} ^{2}$$ . Do not use the Pythagorean Theorem.
Verify the parallelogram law for vectors $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ :

Let $$\mathbf{v} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} a \\ b \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . Describe the set $$H$$ of vectors $$\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} x \\ y \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ that are orthogonal to $$\mathbf{v}$$ . [Hint: Consider $$\mathbf{v} = \textbf{0}$$ and $$\mathbf{v} \neq \textbf{0}$$ .]

Let $$\mathbf{u} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 5 \\ {- 6} \\ 7 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , and let $$W$$ be the set of all $$\textbf{x}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ such that $$\mathbf{u} \cdot \textbf{x} = 0$$ . What theorem in Chapter 4 can be used to show that $$W$$ is a subspace of $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ ? Describe $$W$$ in geometric language.
Suppose a vector $$\textbf{y}$$ is orthogonal to vectors $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ . Show that $$\textbf{y}$$ is orthogonal to the vector $$\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}$$ .

Suppose $$\textbf{y}$$ is orthogonal to $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ . Show that $$\textbf{y}$$ is orthogonal to every $$\textbf{w}$$ in $$\text{Span} \left\{ \mathbf{u} \text{,} \mathbf{v} \right\}$$ . [Hint: An arbitrary $$\textbf{w}$$ in $$\text{Span} \left\{ \mathbf{u} \text{,} \mathbf{v} \right\}$$ has the form $$\textbf{w} = c_{1}\mathbf{u} + c_{2}\mathbf{v}$$ . Show that $$\textbf{y}$$ is orthogonal to such a vector $$\textbf{w}$$ .]

Let $$W = \text{Span} \left\{ \mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,} \ldots \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{p} \right\}$$ . Show that if $$\textbf{x}$$ is orthogonal to each $$\mathbf{v}_{j}$$ , for $$1 \leq j \leq p$$ , then $$\textbf{x}$$ is orthogonal to every vector in $$W$$ .

Let $$W$$ be a subspace of $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , and let $$W^{\bot}$$ be the set of all vectors orthogonal to $$W$$ . Show that $$W^{\bot}$$ is a subspace of $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ using the following steps.
Show that if $$\textbf{x}$$ is in both $$W$$ and $$W^{\bot}$$ , then $$\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$$ .

problem.paragraph: If $$W \neq \left\{ \textbf{0} \right\}$$ , let $$\left\{ \textbf{b}_{1} \text{,} \ldots \text{,} \textbf{b}_{p} \right\}$$ be a basis for $$W$$ , where $$1 \leq p \leq n$$ . Let $$A$$ be the $$p \times n$$ matrix having rows $$\textbf{b}_{1}^{T}$$ , $$\ldots$$ , $$\textbf{b}_{p}^{T}$$ . It follows that $$W$$ is the row space of $$A$$ . Theorem 3 implies that $$W^{\bot} = \left( \text{Row} A)^{\bot} = \text{Nul} A \right.$$ and hence $$\text{dim} W^{\bot} = \text{dim} \text{Nul} A$$ . Thus, $$\text{dim} W + \text{dim} W^{\bot} = \text{dim Row} A + \text{dim Nul} A = \text{rank} A + \text{dim Nul} A = n$$ , by the Rank Theorem. If $$W = \left\{ \textbf{0} \right\}$$ , then $$W^{\bot} = \mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , and the result follows.
